strengths: Clear, well-motivated hypothesis (LLM suggestibility under epistemic uncertainty) that is empirically validated in a preliminary study before the method is introduced, giving the approach a principled grounding rather than being purely ad hoc.

The method (DINCO) is conceptually elegant: it unifies two previously separate lines of work (self-consistency as generation-side coherence, and normalized verbalized confidence as validation-side coherence) via the generator-validator disagreement framing, which is a nice theoretical contribution beyond just an empirical trick.

Extensive experimentation across short-form (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, BioASQ) and long-form (FactScore) tasks, multiple open-source models (Qwen3 1.7B/8B/32B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B) and frontier closed models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash), and both gray-box and black-box settings, demonstrating broad applicability.

Strong set of ablations and robustness checks: NLI model choice, inference budget split, P(True) vs numerical confidence, one-step vs two-step distractor generation/validation, and a FLOP-controlled scaling analysis showing that scaling self-consistency alone cannot match DINCO.

Introduction of a novel and useful diagnostic (confidence saturation, quantified via the ∆ε metric) that provides additional insight into why verbalized confidence is unreliable beyond standard calibration metrics.
Statistical significance testing (bootstrap CIs for ECE/BS, DeLong test for AUC) is included, which is often missing in calibration papers and strengthens the empirical claims.

Good engagement with related work, clearly distinguishing DINCO's independent-prompting approach from prior joint-prompting/top-k confidence elicitation methods, with a clear rationale for why independent prompting better exposes incoherence.
weaknesses: In the black-box setting (no logit access), DINCO's AUC sometimes falls substantially below simpler baselines (e.g., GPT-4.1 on SimpleQA: DINCO_black-box AUC 0.605 vs. SC-VC 0.761 and SC 0.750), yet this notable degradation is only briefly acknowledged in the main text without deeper analysis of why coherence-based normalization fails to help ranking in this regime.

The final combination f^DINCO = 1/2 f^SC + 1/2 f^NVC is a fixed, unweighted average without theoretical justification for equal weighting or exploration of a learned/adaptive combination; the robustness check on budget splits (Appendix D.4) partially compensates but the weighting formula itself is not ablated.

The theoretical derivation in Section 2.1 rests on a fairly strong simplifying assumption (that the suggestibility bias β(c) is approximately constant across a mutually-exclusive claim set), which is plausible but not directly verified, only indirectly supported through downstream calibration results.

Reliance on an external off-the-shelf NLI model for redundancy/contradiction weighting introduces a dependency whose quality is critical (shown by the large ECE degradation in the NLI ablation), and while the authors argue NLI is a 'solved' task, no analysis is given of cases where NLI errors specifically harm calibration (e.g., under domain shift or subtle claims).

Additional inference cost (32% more FLOPs than self-consistency in the main setup, reducible to 10% with the one-step variant) may still be a practical barrier for some deployment settings, and cost-accuracy tradeoffs against stronger, more expensive baselines (e.g., higher-budget SC-VC or ensembles) are not as thoroughly explored as the SC scaling comparison.

Some baseline comparisons are mixed or inconsistent across metrics/settings (e.g., MSP sometimes wins on AUC while losing badly on ECE), and the paper's narrative sometimes emphasizes DINCO's wins while somewhat downplaying these inconsistencies, which could benefit from more balanced discussion.

The method's effectiveness depends on the generator LLM being able to produce plausible, diverse, minimal-pair distractors; while Appendix C.1 provides supportive analysis, there is no systematic failure-mode analysis of what happens when distractor generation is poor (e.g., for very obscure or highly technical claims) beyond the aggregate BioASQ result.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated hypothesis (LLM 'suggestibility' under epistemic uncertainty) that is first validated empirically before the method is introduced, giving the approach a principled grounding rather than being purely heuristic.

The DINCO method is technically well-formulated, with a clean derivation (multiplicative bias model, normalization by distractor confidence) and a sensible mechanism (NLI-based reweighting) for handling redundant/non-contradictory distractors.

Extensive and diverse experimental evaluation: multiple open-source model families/scales (Qwen3-1.7B/8B/32B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B) and frontier closed models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash), short-form QA (TriviaQA, SimpleQA), long-form generation (FactScore biography), and an additional domain-transfer test (BioASQ biomedical QA), plus both white-box and black-box (no logit access) settings.

Strong supporting analyses beyond headline numbers: a novel saturation metric (Δϵ) explaining why DINCO improves usability of confidence scores, a compute-controlled scaling study showing DINCO at 10 calls beats self-consistency at 100, ablations of the NLI component and NLI model choice, budget-split robustness analysis, and a cost-reduced one-step variant.

Significance testing (bootstrap/DeLong tests) is used to support comparisons rather than relying on point estimates alone, and prompts/methodological details are thoroughly documented in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.

The paper situates itself clearly relative to related work on generator-validator disagreement, self-consistency, and joint multi-answer prompting, articulating a clear conceptual distinction (independent vs. joint elicitation) that is also empirically tested.
weaknesses: DINCO's advantage is not uniform across all metrics/settings (e.g., MSP sometimes wins on AUC, SC sometimes wins on AUC/Pearson-r in the FactScore Qwen3-8B setting), so the paper's claims of consistent superiority are only partially supported and require some cherry-picking of which metric to emphasize.

The approach depends on an external NLI model and on beam search/pseudo-beam search for generating minimal-pair distractors; the black-box (no logit access) variant of DINCO performs noticeably worse than the white-box version, suggesting the practical method is less robust when only text I/O is available.

The core assumption that suggestibility bias β(c) is approximately constant across a mutually-exclusive claim set is a strong simplifying assumption that is not directly validated, only indirectly supported via downstream calibration results.

DINCO incurs meaningfully higher inference cost than the strongest baseline (SC), and although a one-step variant reduces this, the reported savings (32%→10% overhead) still add non-trivial cost and engineering complexity (extra NLI scoring, distractor generation prompts) relative to simpler baselines.

Dataset sizes (1000 sampled questions per short-form dataset, 183 entities for FactScore) are moderate, and correctness-as-proxy-for-epistemic-certainty in the preliminary study (Section 2.2) is acknowledged as noisy, somewhat weakening the strength of the core empirical claim underlying the method's motivation.
